lab_title: AR Lab: Apparent Retrograde Motion—Why Mars Loops in the Sky
top_level_objectives: Explain how apparent retrograde motion arises from relative motion between Earth and an outer planet (e.g., Mars).
Compare geocentric-style explanations to heliocentric relative-motion reasoning using an outside-the-solar-system perspective.
Track and interpret Mars’s ~26-month retrograde event as an observable eastward drift, westward loop, and return to eastward motion.
Extend the reasoning to Jupiter and Saturn by predicting how orbital radius affects loop size and retrograde duration.
Connect the observed sky behavior to an intuitive “passing/overtaking” analogy (cars in adjacent lanes) and verify it with the model.

scenes.scene_name: Scene 1: The Night-Sky Puzzle (What Mars Appears to Do)
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the observational pattern of Mars’s retrograde motion and establish the question the lab will answer.
key_visuals: AR sky dome with background constellations
Mars marker that shifts slowly eastward day-to-day
A time-lapse indicator approaching the retrograde period, showing Mars slowing
Labels for “eastward drift” and “westward loop”
student_actions: Observe the time-lapse of Mars over multiple nights and identify when it slows, reverses, and resumes eastward motion.
Record a short prediction of what could cause the reversal (e.g., “Mars turns around,” “Earth changes,” or “something else”).

scenes.scene_name: Scene 2: Measure the Apparent Motion Across Constellations
scenes.brief_purpose: Have students characterize retrograde quantitatively in terms of direction and rate as seen from Earth.
key_visuals: Constellation grid/markers behind Mars’s path
A projected “trail” showing Mars’s apparent path across the same starfield
Arrows indicating instantaneous direction (east vs west) at key times
A slider for “observation dates” across the retrograde interval
student_actions: Using the date control, choose three representative moments: pre-retrograde, mid-loop, and post-retrograde.
For each moment, state the apparent direction of motion relative to the star background and estimate whether Mars’s speed appears faster or slower than usual.
Answer a prompt: “At mid-loop, what must be true about Mars’s apparent motion relative to the stars?”

scenes.scene_name: Scene 3: Geocentric vs Heliocentric Reasoning (The Conceptual Hook)
scenes.brief_purpose: Contrast why geocentric explanations become complex with the heliocentric relative-motion picture that naturally produces loops.
key_visuals: Split-view panels: “Geocentric model” (Earth fixed) and “Heliocentric model” (Earth orbiting)
Geocentric panel shows an artificial-complication visual (e.g., adjustable epicycle-like ring/arrow) to force the loop
Heliocentric panel shows two planets moving on smooth orbits around the Sun
A question prompt overlay: “Which explanation is simpler and why?”
student_actions: Briefly evaluate the plausibility/simplicity of each model based on the visuals: does one require changing parameters to match the loop?
Select which model should produce retrograde naturally without “extra tuning,” and justify in one sentence.

scenes.brief_purpose: Provide the core mechanism: Earth (moving faster on the inner orbit) catches up to Mars, creating the apparent reversal.
key_visuals: Solar-system exterior viewpoint with the Sun at the center
Smooth, labeled circular/elliptical orbits for Earth and Mars
A “relative motion” animation where Earth’s position advances and Mars’s advances more slowly
A tether line or alignment indicator showing when Earth passes Mars in angular position
Optional lane/relative-speed visual metaphor embedded in the scene
student_actions: Identify the moment when Earth is “catching up” to Mars in its orbital path (near the start of the loop).
Determine when Earth passes the aligned position (the loop’s turning behavior) and when Mars resumes apparent eastward motion after separation.
Answer a prompt using the car-lane analogy: “Which object appears to drift backward, and why?”

scenes.scene_name: Scene 5: Map the Mechanism Back to the Sky (Link Outside View to Earth View)
scenes.brief_purpose: Connect the outside-model geometry to the observed sky loop, reinforcing that the loop is an apparent effect.
key_visuals: Side-by-side: left is outside view (Earth/Mars orbit positions), right is Earth-view sky with Mars path
A synchronization cue: the same time stamp highlighted on both panels
Arcs showing line-of-sight direction from Earth to Mars in the sky-view panel
A “phase angle” label indicating changing relative alignment
student_actions: At two or three synchronized timestamps, match an outside-view configuration to the corresponding point on the sky loop (early loop, mid-loop, recovery).
Explain how the line-of-sight direction changes even when Mars’s physical motion stays smooth.
Answer: “Is Mars actually reversing? What changes in the observer’s frame?”

scenes.scene_name: Scene 6: Predicting Retrograde for Jupiter and Saturn (How Distance Changes the Effect)
scenes.brief_purpose: Generalize the mechanism by comparing orbital speeds and relative angular motion for other outer planets.
key_visuals: AR sky view or orbit view with Jupiter and Saturn added alongside Mars
Smaller loop paths for Jupiter and Saturn compared with Mars on the same scale
A relative-speed indicator showing Earth overtakes them more slowly in angular terms
A control to toggle between planets and display their loop amplitude/duration
student_actions: Use the model to observe Jupiter and Saturn’s retrograde loops and compare loop size and duration to Mars.
Predict (before observing or after brief observation) which planet should show the smallest loop and provide the relative-motion reason.
Conclude with a rule-of-thumb: “As orbital radius increases, what happens to retrograde amplitude and why?”
